sources.title: Why the Godfather of A.I. Fears What He's Built
sources.speaker: Geoffrey Hinton (interviewed by Joshua Rothman, The New Yorker)
sources.locator: Full profile; reporting visit to Hinton's Georgian Bay island (the profile does not state how long; the text shows at least an overnight stay: 'the next morning', 'Late in the day'). Key passages: family-tree/father section ('If you work twice as hard as me'), woodwork vs science ('mostly anxiety'), tree-felling and contractor-notes section, Rosalind and Jackie sections, Boltzmann Machine section, closing 'unplug it' exchange
sources.excerpt: "I've often wondered whether I'd have been happier as an architect, because I didn't have to force myself to do it. Whereas, with science, I've always had to force myself. Because of the family, I had to succeed at it—I had to find a path. There was joy in it, but it was mostly anxiety. Now it's an enormous relief that I've succeeded."
sources.context: Long-form magazine profile built on in-person reporting at Hinton's cottage in 2023, months after he left Google. Hinton's own words are quoted at length; the reporter's scene-setting and interpretations (e.g. 'The tree was an error') are Rothman's, not Hinton's. Canonical page opened by plain curl and checked against a full-text PDF copy; key quotations confirmed on the canonical page. Same visit also yields S02 testimony, so S01 and S02 are not independent of each other.

sources.title: Why the Godfather of A.I. Fears What He's Built (third-party testimony within the profile)

sources.context: Named testimony from a former student/collaborator who publicly disagrees with Hinton about AI risk (LeCun), a co-laureate (Bengio), and his partner (Gartner). Same article as S01, so it is not independent reporting; it is independent voice.

claims.inference: Synthesizes C10, C11, C64, C22, C25, C15 and C08. Medium confidence. 'Costliest' was replaced by 'most telling' because several items cost him little (critic-02).
claims.alternative: Curiosity (Type 5), professional demand, goodwill toward Google and ordinary integrity explain parts of the same record. The Gebru episode shows the reflex is selective and partly tied to career stage; the article states this limit in the Google section.

claims.claim: Type answer (interpretation): Type 1, medium confidence, Type 5 the serious rival.
claims.passage: Ones live by an inner standard of how things should be.
claims.inference: Plain-language statement of the leading hypothesis, with confidence and rival stated in the same answer.
claims.alternative: See type_hypothesis.against and alternative_case.

claims.claim: Hinton recalls his father, the entomologist Howard Everest Hinton, saying: 'If you work twice as hard as me, when you're twice as old as I am you might be half as good' (New Yorker, 2023).
claims.passage: If you work twice as hard as me, when you're twice as old as I am you might be half as good.
claims.inference: Establishes a demanding paternal standard Hinton still cites in his seventies. It is consistent with an internalized critical standard (Type 1), but equally with achievement pressure (Type 3) or anxiety (Type 6).
claims.alternative: Two wordings exist; quote each exactly with its source. A childhood standard is context, not proof of type; do not frame it as a causal wound.

claims.claim: Hinton told 60 Minutes (2023) of his father: 'He knew a lot more about beetles than he knew about people.'
claims.passage: He knew a lot more about beetles than he knew about people
claims.inference: His characterization of a distant father.
claims.alternative: One remark; context, not a causal wound.

claims.claim: After his father died, the study was lined with boxes of beetle papers, with a smaller box near the door labeled 'Not insects' that held the family papers.
claims.passage: slightly smaller box that simply said, 'Not insects,' and that's where he had all the things about the family.
claims.inference: A concrete, memorable detail of a father organized around work; used for the section title.
claims.alternative: Hinton's recollection on 60 Minutes; not interpreted as a type marker.

claims.claim: Hinton's father, a committed Communist (the New Yorker says Stalinist), forbade him to study biology for ideological reasons; remembering this, Hinton said 'I hate faiths of all kinds.'
claims.passage: I hate faiths of all kinds.
claims.inference: Strong aversion to belief held without evidence. That fits an internal standard of correctness (1), skepticism (6) or a reasoning-first temperament (5).
claims.alternative: One remark in context of a specific childhood conflict. The draft's gloss ('genetics cut against the belief that human nature could be remade') paraphrases the New Yorker's explanation of the father's view.

claims.claim: Nobel Week (Dec 2024): 'There was a lot of pressure to succeed academically, so I kind of knew from a very early age that I had to be a successful academic or a failure.'
claims.passage: I had to be a successful academic or a failure
claims.inference: Self-report of an early, binary standard.
claims.alternative: External achievement pressure; the article uses it in the Type 3 paragraph and does not score it for Type 1.

claims.claim: Hinton told the New Yorker he wondered whether he'd have been happier as an architect 'because I didn't have to force myself to do it', whereas with science 'I've always had to force myself. Because of the family, I had to succeed at it—I had to find a path. There was joy in it, but it was mostly anxiety. Now it's an enormous relief that I've succeeded.'
claims.passage: There was joy in it, but it was mostly anxiety.
claims.inference: Hinton describes science as forced and 'mostly anxiety'. The article's closing line keeps his own word ('anxiety') and treats the pressure as fitting 1, 3 and 6 alike.
claims.alternative: Retrospective self-description by a man who, by students' accounts (C07), visibly enjoyed research. 'Successful academic or failure' comes from auto-captions ('ailure'); recheck against audio before quoting.

claims.claim: Of carpentry, Hinton told SVT on Nobel banquet night: 'there was never any pressure with carpentry. I'm not very good at it, but I enjoy it.'
claims.passage: there was never any pressure with carpentry. I'm not very good at it, but I enjoy it
claims.inference: The chosen-versus-required split in his own words.
claims.alternative: Audio-verified; the audio begins 'Yeah,' which the draft omits at the start of the quoted fragment.

claims.claim: SVT (Dec 2024): 'My parents were atheists and sent me to a Christian school and I was the only person who didn't believe in God. As time went by, it turned out I was right.' He said being surrounded by people he thought were wrong 'was very useful when I was studying neural nets.'
claims.passage: I was the only person who didn't believe in God. As time went by, it turned out I was right
claims.inference: Cross-context self-description of holding a view against the room.
claims.alternative: Audio-verified. Retrospective, told by a man proven right.

claims.claim: Asked by 60 Minutes when he realized he had been right about neural networks, Hinton said: 'I always thought I was right.'
claims.passage: I always thought I was right
claims.inference: Repeated, cross-context self-description that rightness is something he sees internally and holds against consensus. That fits a Type 1 internal authority and also Type 5 trust in one's own model. It is a weak fit with Type 6, who typically seeks outside confirmation.
claims.alternative: Could be the retrospective confidence of a man proven right, not a lifelong trait. Professional incentive: the 'lone right scientist' story is also a good public narrative.

claims.claim: New Yorker: 'I was always convinced it wasn't nonsense. It wasn't really faith—it was just completely obvious to me.'
claims.passage: It wasn't really faith—it was just completely obvious to me.
claims.inference: Rightness experienced as plain sight rather than belief; fits an internal standard (1) or trust in one's own model (5).
claims.alternative: Retrospective.

claims.claim: Nobel Week (Dec 2024) advice: if an idea seems right and differs from what everybody believes, 'don't give up on it until you've figured out why it's wrong' and 'you should just ignore what other people say. I'm very good at ignoring what other people say.'
claims.passage: I'm very good at ignoring what other people say.
claims.inference: A repeated rule of conduct (October and December 2024). It shows a standard tested against his own reasoning, not against social approval.
claims.alternative: Generic advice many laureates give. Audio-verified; the audio reads 'you've figured out' (captions 'you figured out').

claims.claim: Hinton on the Boltzmann Machine: 'It should be true ... If I was God, I'd make it true.'
claims.passage: If I was God, I'd make it true.
claims.inference: An aesthetic 'should' about a theory. The article labels it as a theorist's taste that a Five's love of elegant models explains as well as a One's standard; it is not used as a One discriminator.
claims.alternative: The quotes are about algorithms, not morality; reading 'should' as typological is interpretive.

claims.claim: Yann LeCun, Hinton's former student and collaborator: 'Geoff thought it was the most beautiful algorithm. I thought it was ugly.'
claims.passage: Geoff thought it was the most beautiful algorithm. I thought it was ugly.
claims.inference: Independent voice confirming Hinton's aesthetic attachment to the Boltzmann Machine.
claims.alternative: Same article as S01; LeCun's role is the New Yorker's description ('a former student and collaborator').

claims.claim: Bengio recalls Hinton, as an external reviewer of his master's thesis, writing 'something like "This should not work"'; the method worked better than Hinton expected.
claims.passage: something like 'This should not work.'
claims.inference: A predictive 'should'. Labeled non-discriminating in the article.
claims.alternative: Bengio's paraphrase of a decades-old review comment.

claims.claim: Of backpropagation: 'It's so unsatisfying intellectually ... Unfortunately, it just works better.'
claims.passage: Unfortunately, it just works better.
claims.inference: He abandoned the algorithm he loved for the one that worked. The article presents this as the Five's move, not as One evidence.
claims.alternative: Algorithmic taste, not morality; reading 'should' as typological is interpretive (labeled as such in the draft).

claims.claim: On his Georgian Bay island the New Yorker reports contractors' 'needless mistakes (running a drainage pipe uphill, leaving floors half finished) that still enrage him today' and that 'Almost every room harbors a corrective mini-project'.
claims.passage: made needless mistakes (running a drainage pipe uphill, leaving floors half finished) that still enrage him today.
claims.inference: Non-professional evidence of irritation at other people's carelessness and of a repeated urge to bring a place into line. The article attributes 'enrage' to Rothman explicitly and dates the observation to the 2023 visit.
claims.alternative: One reporter's visit (stated in the article: 'This rests on one reporter's visit'). 'Enrage' is Rothman's narration, not Hinton's words. Precision about building work is also ordinary in an engineer (5).

claims.claim: The New Yorker's Joshua Rothman visited Hinton on his Georgian Bay island in 2023.
claims.passage: visited Hinton on his island in Georgian Bay, Ontario
claims.inference: Scope and limit of the home evidence: one reporter's visit. No duration is given because S01 does not state one (repair of verify-01).
claims.alternative: None; scene-setting fact. The article separately flags that the home evidence rests on one reporter's visit.

claims.claim: Rothman: 'On the island, he is always cutting down trees to create more orderly and beautiful tableaus.'
claims.passage: he is always cutting down trees to create more orderly and beautiful tableaus
claims.inference: Reporter's observation of an ordering habit.
claims.alternative: Reporter's characterization; see C08 on the published correction about the felling process.

claims.claim: Hinton's notes to contractors were written on the materials, e.g. 'Bathroom should have this type of baseboard (maple trim in front of shower only)' and 'Do not prime shelf, prime shelf support.'
claims.passage: Do not prime shelf, prime shelf support.
claims.inference: Concrete corrective behavior at home.
claims.alternative: Notes to a new contractor are also practical; the draft says the anger, not the notes, is the tell.

claims.claim: When his third wife Jackie, ill with pancreatic cancer, could no longer manage the cottage stairs, Hinton built a basket on a string so she could lower her tea to be warmed in the microwave; he observed, 'I should've just moved the microwave upstairs.'
claims.passage: I should've just moved the microwave upstairs.
claims.inference: Even a tender story ends in a self-correction; texture for the corrective habit.
claims.alternative: Dry humor, not necessarily self-criticism. Concerns a deceased private person; kept brief and in his framing.

claims.claim: In December 2012 Hinton ran the auction for DNNresearch, a three-person company, from room 731 of Harrah's at Lake Tahoe.
claims.passage: In December 2012, Hinton ran an auction for a three-person company, DNNresearch, from room 731 of Harrah's at Lake Tahoe.
claims.inference: Factual frame for the auction anecdotes.
claims.alternative: Metz's reconstruction; company name confirmed by Hinton on Diary of a CEO.

claims.claim: Hinton says he sold his company to a big company because 'I have a son who has learning difficulties and in order to be sure he would never be out on the street I needed to get several million dollars and I wasn't going to get that as an academic.' He had tried teaching a Coursera course for money first.
claims.passage: I have a son who has learning difficulties
claims.inference: A security-and-responsibility motive for the most lucrative decision of his life, given in his own words.
claims.alternative: Sensitive: concerns a private living family member. Used only in Hinton's own public framing, once, without further detail. Retrospective 2025 account; audio-verified.

claims.claim: Per Metz, when Baidu's Kai Yu left his backpack in room 731, Hinton and his students considered looking inside for bid information but 'knowing it wasn't the right thing to do, they didn't.'
claims.passage: knowing it wasn't the right thing to do, they didn't
claims.inference: The backpack decision and stopping short of the maximum price show rule-keeping and 'right home' over money (consistent with 1). Hiding frailty to protect his image is a point for 3, not 1.
claims.alternative: Metz's narration, not a Hinton quote; the draft labels it so.

claims.claim: Hinton stopped the auction as the price hit $44 million and sold to Google.
claims.passage: as the price hit $44 million, Hinton stopped the auction and sold to Google
claims.inference: Choosing a buyer over a higher price.
claims.alternative: Metz's reconstruction; other practical factors are possible.

claims.claim: Metz: 'finding the right home for his research was ultimately more important to him than commanding the maximum price.'
claims.passage: finding the right home for his research was ultimately more important to him than commanding the maximum price
claims.inference: Author's motive attribution, labeled in the draft as Metz's reading.
claims.alternative: Not Hinton's words.

claims.claim: Hinton hid a makeshift humidifying chamber from Baidu's visitor: 'I didn't want them thinking I was old and decrepit.'
claims.passage: I didn't want them thinking I was old and decrepit
claims.inference: Image management: a point for Type 3, reported in the draft as counterevidence.
claims.alternative: Ordinary dealmaking prudence is also possible.

claims.claim: He told his students, while they hid it: 'This is what vice presidents do.'
claims.passage: This is what vice presidents do
claims.inference: Dry humor in the same episode.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Hinton left Google in spring 2023, at 75.
claims.passage: Hinton left Google in spring 2023, at 75.
claims.inference: Dates the departure.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Days before the announcement, MIT Technology Review: 'I want to talk about AI safety issues without having to worry about how it interacts with Google's business ... As long as I'm paid by Google, I can't do that.'
claims.passage: As long as I'm paid by Google, I can't do that.
claims.inference: His 2023 account of leaving.
claims.alternative: The 2025 account puts age first (C58).

claims.claim: Diary of a CEO (June 2025): 'The main reason I left Google was because I was 75 and I wanted to retire. I've done a very bad job of that.'
claims.passage: The main reason I left Google was because I was 75 and I wanted to retire.
claims.inference: A less heroic account that the draft reports alongside the principled one.
claims.alternative: Audio-verified.

claims.claim: He also said he was 'making many more mistakes when I programmed, which is very annoying.'
claims.passage: making many more mistakes when I programmed, which is very annoying
claims.inference: Irritation at his own declining precision; cited in the Five discriminator as irritation at carelessness, including his own.
claims.alternative: Audio-verified.

claims.claim: Google encouraged him to stay and work on AI safety and said he could do whatever he liked on it.
claims.passage: Google, he said, had encouraged him to stay and work on safety.
claims.inference: Shows the exit was not forced.
claims.alternative: His account; Google's side not checked.

claims.claim: On why he would not stay: 'You kind of censor yourself if you work for a big company, you don't feel right saying things that will damage the big company. Even if you could get away with it, it just feels wrong to me.'
claims.passage: Even if you could get away with it, it just feels wrong to me.
claims.inference: Felt wrongness about conduct ('it just feels wrong to me'), the strongest first-person One-vs-Five discriminator in the record.
claims.alternative: The 2025 account puts age first, so the exit was not purely principled. Retirement plus the wish to speak freely is an ordinary career transition.

claims.claim: Hinton in 2025: 'So I feel I have a duty now to talk about the risks.'
claims.passage: So I feel I have a duty now to talk about the risks
claims.inference: Duty language for his advocacy.
claims.alternative: Audio-verified.

claims.claim: On October 8, 2024 Hinton said he would 'spend my time advocating for people to work on safety.'
claims.passage: I'm going to spend my time advocating for people to work on safety.
claims.inference: A repeated, costly choice of public duty over rest. It is central to the Type 1 reading (reformer acting on a 'should') and harder to square with a withdrawing Type 5, though a healthy 5 moving toward 8 could also explain it.
claims.alternative: Late-career roles are also shaped by demand; Nobel prestige makes him sought after. Audio-verified.

claims.claim: At his October 8, 2024 Nobel press conference Hinton said: 'I'm particularly proud of the fact that one of my students fired Sam Altman.'
claims.passage: I'm particularly proud of the fact that one of my students fired Sam Altman
claims.inference: He makes blunt public moral judgments of powerful people. That fits a Type 1 judging mind (and an 8-like bluntness), and he declines to judge someone he doesn't know.
claims.alternative: Opinion about a living person; the draft attributes it to Hinton and adds dated context on the 2023 removal and reinstatement (C69), including Sutskever's later apology. Musk remarks are not used.

claims.claim: Asked to elaborate, he said OpenAI was set up with a big emphasis on safety and 'over time, it turned out that Sam Altman was much less concerned with safety than with profits. And I think that's unfortunate.'
claims.passage: much less concerned with safety than with profits
claims.inference: A blunt moral judgment of a powerful person.
claims.alternative: Hinton's opinion; attributed as his view.

claims.claim: OpenAI's board removed Sam Altman as CEO on November 17, 2023, after concerns led by Ilya Sutskever and Mira Murati; Sutskever later publicly apologized for his part, and Altman was reinstated on November 22, 2023.
claims.passage: Sutskever later apologized publicly for his part, and Altman was reinstated on November 22
claims.inference: Context for Hinton's remark.
claims.alternative: Reference summary; motives for the removal remain disputed. The article now gives the board's stated reason and the March 2024 investigation finding (C110, C111) so Hinton's safety-versus-profit view stays his own.

claims.claim: Hinton backed Encode's December 2024 amicus brief opposing OpenAI's proposed for-profit conversion: 'OpenAI was founded as an explicitly safety-focused nonprofit and made a variety of safety-related promises in its charter ... Allowing it to tear all of that up when it becomes inconvenient sends a very bad message to other actors in the ecosystem.'
claims.passage: Allowing it to tear all of that up when it becomes inconvenient sends a very bad message to other actors in the ecosystem.
claims.inference: He objects to promises being torn up when keeping them becomes inconvenient. Normative language about conduct, used in the Five discriminator. The article does not say OpenAI broke a promise; it reports his objection to a proposal and then the dated outcome (C112, C113).
claims.alternative: A policy position shared by many safety advocates; may reflect alliance-building as much as temperament. OpenAI later kept nonprofit control (May and October 2025), so the article frames this as his December 2024 objection only.
claims.review_trigger: Re-check if OpenAI's control structure changes again (state as of S25, 2025-10-28: public benefit corporation under nonprofit control) or the Musk v. OpenAI litigation produces a final ruling.

claims.claim: Asked on October 8, 2024 how he would describe himself: 'I would say I am someone who doesn't really know what field he's in but would like to understand how the brain works.'
claims.passage: I would say I am someone who doesn't really know what field he's in but would like to understand how the brain works
claims.inference: This is the strongest evidence for Type 5: a lifelong driving question about how minds work. Under the Type 1 reading, the question is the vocation and the internal standard is the engine.
claims.alternative: Taken alone, this points to 5.

claims.claim: Hinton theorizes emotion: 'I think feelings are counterfactual statements about what would have caused an action.'
claims.passage: I think feelings are counterfactual statements about what would have caused an action
claims.inference: Translating feelings into mechanism is a classic Type 5 move: understanding emotion by modeling it. This is counterevidence for the leading Type 1 read.
claims.alternative: It is also simply his scientific position on AI and minds, held for professional reasons.

claims.claim: Hinton says his turn to safety came from understanding: 'The closest I had to a eureka moment was when a Google system called Palm was able to say why a joke was funny,' coupled with realizing how much better digital is than analog for sharing information.
claims.passage: The closest I had to a eureka moment was when a Google system called Palm was able to say why a joke was funny
claims.inference: The fear follows a model conclusion. That is a point for 5 (and for 1's evidence-first rightness) against an anxiety-first Type 6 reading.
claims.alternative: He also says he wishes he had worried sooner (S08); the 'oxy moron' anecdote is not used in the draft. Audio-verified.

claims.claim: Of his 2016 prediction that AI would by now be reading all the scans radiologists read: 'That prediction was wrong. I was a bit overenthusiastic.'
claims.passage: That prediction was wrong. I was a bit overenthusiastic
claims.inference: He updates easily and without visible self-flagellation. That reads as a model-updater (Type 5), and it is counterevidence for the harsh self-criticism often associated with Type 1.
claims.alternative: Admitting error is also a credibility tool for a public warner. Audio-verified (captions read 'over enthusiastic').

claims.claim: MIT Technology Review (2023): asked whether he was an optimist or a pessimist, Hinton said, 'I'm mildly depressed ... Which is why I'm scared.' Just before, he framed the mildly depressed as the people whose risk estimates are 'usually right'.
claims.passage: "I'm mildly depressed," he said. "Which is why I'm scared."
claims.inference: Real fear, which supports a Type 6 alternative, but he presents it as following from an estimate of the odds rather than as free-floating dread. The article now quotes the fear in full rather than contrasting calibration with dread (verify-03).
claims.alternative: Anticipatory fear plus practical hedging (C70) is the strongest Six evidence. Hedging against a modeled risk is also what a Type 5 or 1 would do once convinced.

claims.claim: He spreads his and his children's money between three Canadian banks in case a cyberattack takes one down.
claims.passage: spreads his money and his children's money between three Canadian banks
claims.inference: Concrete hedging: the strongest Type 6 datum.
claims.alternative: Hedging a modeled risk is also what a 5 or 1 would do once convinced. Audio-verified.

claims.claim: On estimates of bad outcomes, the mildly depressed person 'will say the odds are maybe around 40%, and they're usually right.'
claims.passage: the mildly depressed are "usually right."
claims.inference: He frames his gloom as an estimate of the odds; in the same passage he connects it to being scared (C21).
claims.alternative: His heuristic, not evidence that his estimates are right; the fear he attaches to it remains Six-compatible.

claims.claim: Chris Maddison: 'He was famous for bursting into a room and pronouncing that, he now finally, after all these years, understood how the brain worked.'
claims.passage: He was famous for bursting into a room and pronouncing that, he now finally, after all these years, understood how the brain worked.
claims.inference: Independent named testimony of delight in ideas and warmth toward students. This is counterevidence to the 'mostly anxiety' self-report (C03) and to a detached Type 5 caricature, and it is a playful texture a strict Type 1 reading does not predict.
claims.alternative: Celebratory university article; affectionate by design. The Asteroids injury is Frosst's secondhand retelling.

claims.claim: Maddison: 'The excitement, the joy radiated out of his office down the hall.'
claims.passage: The excitement, the joy radiated out of his office down the hall
claims.inference: Counterevidence to the 'mostly anxiety' self-report.
claims.alternative: Celebratory university article.

claims.claim: Hinton told the New Yorker that 'Geoff' is an anagram for 'ego fortissimo'.
claims.passage: 'Geoff' is an anagram for 'ego fortissimo.'
claims.inference: Irreverent, anti-authority wit. Sharp one-liners fit a Type 1 critic's dry edge and a counterphobic Type 6, and the playfulness also brushes Type 7.
claims.alternative: Humor is weak type evidence.

claims.claim: Hinton replied to a long note from a Canadian intelligence agency with 'Snowden is my hero.'
claims.passage: Snowden is my hero.
claims.inference: Anti-authority wit.
claims.alternative: New Yorker report of an email.

claims.claim: Partner Rosemary Gartner, a retired sociologist: 'I think he's the kind of person who always needs a partner.'
claims.passage: I think he's the kind of person who always needs a partner.
claims.inference: Cuts against a self-sufficient, low-need Type 5 caricature.
claims.alternative: Intimate, affectionate witness. The article dates the relationship to the 2023 visit rather than stating it as current.
claims.review_trigger: Relationship dated to the New Yorker's 2023 visit ('For the past four years'); re-check at the next refresh or if reporting indicates the relationship has changed.

claims.claim: The NYT reported in May 2023: 'A part of him, he said, now regrets his life's work.'
claims.passage: A part of him, he said, now regrets his life's work
claims.inference: Reporter's paraphrase of his regret, quoted as the paper's wording.
claims.alternative: Hinton's later statements soften this (C20, C67).

claims.claim: NYT quote: 'I console myself with the normal excuse: If I hadn't done it, somebody else would have.'
claims.passage: I console myself with the normal excuse: If I hadn't done it, somebody else would have.
claims.inference: His own 2023 words on responsibility.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: By fall 2023 Hinton had sent a journalist a link to Edith Piaf's 'Non, Je Ne Regrette Rien'; the New Yorker says he does not regret his work.
claims.passage: Non, Je Ne Regrette Rien
claims.inference: Low guilt about past work.
claims.alternative: Reported by the New Yorker; the journalist is unnamed.

claims.claim: In 2025 Hinton said: 'I don't feel particularly guilty about developing AI like 40 years ago because at that time we had no idea that this stuff was gonna happen this fast.'
claims.passage: I don't feel particularly guilty about developing AI like 40 years ago
claims.inference: Most of his statements converge on no personal guilt for past work plus a forward-looking duty. Duty-without-guilt fits a principled reformer. The relative absence of self-reproach is counterevidence to a classic Type 1 inner critic.
claims.alternative: Audio-verified. Present as change over time, not contradiction.

claims.claim: Hinton in 2025: 'I wish I'd spent more time with my wife. And with my children when they were little. I was kind of obsessed with work.' He identifies the wife as the one who died of pancreatic cancer (Jackie).
claims.passage: I wish I'd spent more time with my wife.
claims.inference: Work obsession at a family cost, with late regret. It fits a duty-and-standard engine (1), mind-absorption (5) or achievement (3) equally; this is the cost side of the pattern, not a discriminator.
claims.alternative: Audio-verified (captions read 'I wish I spent'). Common regret among high achievers.

claims.claim: He added that Jackie 'was very supportive of me spending a lot of time working.'
claims.passage: was very supportive of me spending a lot of time working.
claims.inference: Context for the regret.
claims.alternative: Audio-verified.

claims.claim: Hinton told the New Yorker that when Rosalind asked him to sell their house to pay for further homeopathic treatment, he refused for the children's sake: 'I drew the line there.'
claims.passage: I drew the line there.
claims.inference: Shows how he responds to irrationality in someone he loves: anger and a firm line set for the children's sake. It also shows him generalizing grief into a principle about facing reality, which reads as both 1 (the right response) and 5 (the rational stance).
claims.alternative: Told only from Hinton's side about a private medical decision of a deceased person. The article adds the New Yorker's mitigating context (C116), removes the 'rational' Jackie contrast, and passes no judgment on Rosalind in the author's voice.

claims.claim: Rosalind died in 1994.
claims.passage: She died in 1994.
claims.inference: Date fact.
claims.alternative: None.

claims.claim: Hinton draws the AI lesson himself: 'We can't be in denial ... We have to be real.'
claims.passage: We can't be in denial
claims.inference: Grief generalized into a principle about facing reality.
claims.alternative: Reads as both 1 and 5.

claims.claim: Half his Nobel share went to a Canadian organization that trains people in Indigenous communities to produce safe drinking water.
claims.passage: trains people living in Indigenous communities to produce safe drinking water
claims.inference: Moral indignation at a fixable injustice, acted on.
claims.alternative: Audio-verified; the organization is not named in the interview.

claims.claim: Hinton's figure: in Ontario 20 percent of Indigenous communities lack safe drinking water.
claims.passage: His figure, in December 2024, was that 20 percent of Indigenous communities in Ontario lacked it.
claims.inference: Attributed as his figure.
claims.alternative: Not independently checked; the article labels it as his figure and dates it to December 2024, so it no longer reads as a current statistic.

claims.claim: 'It's ridiculous at this time in a rich country like Canada ... That's just crazy.'
claims.passage: That's just crazy.
claims.inference: Heat attached to a wrong.
claims.alternative: Audio-verified.

claims.claim: Hinton and Terry Sejnowski agreed in the 1980s to split any prize one of them won for the Boltzmann work; when the 2024 Nobel came, partly for Boltzmann machines, Hinton offered Sejnowski half.
claims.passage: We had an agreement back in the 1980s which was that if they gave it to one of us and not the other one, we'd split it
claims.inference: Keeping a forty-year-old informal promise at real cost, and moral indignation ('crazy') at a fixable injustice. These are among the strongest concrete Type 1 data points.
claims.alternative: Generosity and loyalty also fit 2, 6 or 9. Audio-verified.

claims.claim: Sejnowski declined the money because the prize was also for later work he was not involved in.
claims.passage: Sejnowski declined, because the prize also covered later work he had not been part of.
claims.inference: Hinton's account of Sejnowski's reason.
claims.alternative: Hinton's paraphrase of Sejnowski.

claims.claim: They used that half to set up a prize in Sejnowski's name 'for young researchers with crazy theories of how the brain works, like we were.'
claims.passage: for young researchers with crazy theories of how the brain works, like we were.

type_hypothesis.against: The most obvious read of Hinton is Type 5, and real evidence supports it. He defines himself by a question ('would like to understand how the brain works', C06), theorizes feelings as mechanisms (C27), updates calmly when wrong (C26, C44), and reached his AI fear through a model (C29, C108). His aesthetic and predictive 'shoulds' about algorithms (C28, C43) fit a Five's love of elegant models as well as a One's standard. Against the corrective rule: he stayed silent through a decade at Google, including Timnit Gebru's 2020 ouster, and ranked Gebru's concerns as different from his (C109, C110), so the reflex is selective and partly tied to career stage. Much of the record is post-2023 self-report after being proven right. Against Type 1 specifically: his guilt about his life's work is low (C20, C67), though he regrets the timing (C117) and shows guilt in grief (C119); he is playful and irreverent (C07, C16); he calls science 'mostly anxiety' (C03), an outside pressure that fits 3 or 6; he hedges against threats (C70); he hid his frailty from bidders to protect his image (C51); and the lesson he drew from loss is stoic acceptance, not correction (C120). His first-person anger is mild (C121); 'enrage' is a reporter's word (C08).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 5, the investigator: a lifelong drive to understand how minds work, pursued for fifty years against a dismissive field, with worth anchored in having the right model. It explains his self-description, his analysis-driven fear (C29, C108), his intellectualizing of emotion (C27), his dropping the beloved Boltzmann Machine for backprop (C44), his work absorption at his family's expense (C19) and the island retreat. Fives can also be outspoken public critics, so speaking out does not rule it out. Type 3 (achievement pressure C38, relief at success C03, humidifier concealment C51) ranks below Five because his best-known public moments go against image (C10, C58; C125). Counterphobic Type 6 (lone unbeliever C41, 'I hate faiths' C17, three banks C70, the security-driven sale C14) ranks third: his disagreements follow his model and side with institutions when the model does (C126). Eight is addressed via his mild anger and pattern of leaving institutions rather than running them (C122).
type_hypothesis.discriminator: Not whether he speaks out, which a Five can do, but the voice he acts in. A Five speaks from the authority of the model. Hinton also speaks about conduct, in first-person normative language: criticizing an employer on its payroll 'just feels wrong to me' even if he could get away with it (C11); his advocacy is a 'duty' (C64, C22); OpenAI should not tear up promises 'when it becomes inconvenient' (C25); and he is irritated by carelessness, others' (C08, attributed to Rothman) and his own (C59). That is how a One's held-down anger usually shows. Supporting but non-discriminating: the Times correction (C10, accuracy as much as morality), keeping the Sejnowski promise (C15, principled people of every type keep promises), and the pre-fame Pentagon reason (C127, his accounts differ). Limits: the Gebru silence (C109, C110) narrows the rule to wrongs his own standard selects; fame creates demand; home details rest on one visit; a healthy Five can grow outspoken.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The exuberant, almost Seven-like delight students describe (C07, C73). His low guilt about his life's work and 'Non, Je Ne Regrette Rien' (C20, C67), though he regrets the timing (C117). His self-report that science was 'mostly anxiety' (C03). The image-protective concealment at the 2012 auction (C51), which looks more like Type 3. The stoic acceptance he drew from his wives' deaths (C120), closer to acceptance than correction. The selective Google-era silence (C109, C110). No wing or subtype is proposed.
